In `match` mode the first line is the pattern and every later line is a candidate path; print one line per candidate, `+ `, then the candidate, when it matches, and `- `, then the candidate, when it does not. A pattern with no candidates prints nothing. Exit 0 on success.

Brace expansion runs before matching, and a pattern matches when any of its expansions does. Find the leftmost `{` that has a matching `}`, counting nesting and skipping any character preceded by a backslash. Split the text between them on the commas that sit at that group's own nesting depth, again skipping escaped characters. If there is at least one such comma, the parts are the alternatives, and an alternative may be empty. If there is none, read the body as a range: `A..B` or `A..B..S` where both endpoints are integers, optionally signed, or both are single ASCII letters. Values run from the first endpoint towards the second, inclusive, walking code points for letters, so `{e..a}` counts down and `{A..d}` passes through the characters that lie between `Z` and `a`. An integer range pads its values with leading zeros to the width of the longer endpoint's digits when either endpoint is written with a leading zero, placing the sign before the padding. A body that is neither a list nor a range leaves its braces as literal text, and the search for the next group resumes just after that `{`. A `{` with no matching `}` is literal too. Each alternative is substituted for the whole group and the result expanded again, so the leftmost group varies slowest.

Matching splits both the pattern and the path on `/`, skipping an escaped `/`, and compares segment by segment; a pattern segment that is exactly `**` instead matches zero or more whole path segments, none of which may begin with `.`. Any other segment must match its path segment as a whole. Within a segment, `\` makes the next character literal, `?` matches exactly one character, and any run of `*` matches zero or more characters. A bracket class opens with `[`, is negated by a leading `!` or `^`, holds single characters and `from-to` code-point ranges, treats a `]` written first as a literal, treats a `-` that has no character after it as a literal, honours a backslash inside itself, and closes at the first `]` that is neither first nor escaped. A path segment that begins with `.` matches only a pattern segment whose first element is a literal `.`, written plainly or escaped; a wildcard, a class or a group at the start of a segment never matches that dot. You implement one program task in the workspace you are given, against its own test suite, and you stop when the tests pass.

The workspace is your working directory: every bash command and every file path resolves inside it, so read and edit its files by their relative paths and never search outside it.


Use the read tool — not shell commands like cat — to inspect text files. Results include line numbers. Use offset and limit to continue reading large files.

Use the write tool to create files or completely replace file contents. Existing files are overwritten, so read an existing file first (the default fs-observation-policy requires it) and prefer edit for targeted changes.

Use the edit tool for targeted changes to existing UTF-8 text files. It replaces literal old_string with new_string; by default old_string must appear exactly once. If old_string appears multiple times, provide a more specific old_string or set replace_all to true. Read the file first (the default fs-observation-policy requires it), unless you just created or edited it in this session.

Check the [exit code: N] marker on every bash result; investigate failures before moving on.

Track every background job id you start. You are notified in-session when a job finishes — do not busy-poll or sleep on one; keep working on independent steps and do not duplicate a running job's work. Before giving a final answer, collect every still-relevant job with job_output (set wait: true only when you are genuinely blocked on it), and job_kill jobs that stopped mattering.

tools.name: bash
tools.description: Execute a bash command (`bash -c`) and return its stdout/stderr. Each call runs in a fresh shell: no state (cwd, variables, functions) persists between calls — pass `workdir` instead of using `cd`. Non-zero exits are reported as `[exit code: N]`. Current harness environment facts are exposed through managed `$DSH_*` variables; inspect them when needed. Commands may run under a file sandbox; a blocked file operation is reported as `[sandbox: file access denied under <mode> mode]` — a policy denial, not a bug in the command; do not retry another way. Long output is truncated to its tail; the full output is saved to a file whose path is reported when available. Set `run_in_background: true` for long-running commands: the call returns a job id immediately; read its output with `job_output` and stop it with `job_kill`. Attempting a command the sandbox may deny is safe and expected: run it and read the marker rather than assuming the denial. When a command is denied and a wider mode would let it succeed, escalate immediately in the same turn — the one sanctioned exception to a denial: retry the exact same command once with `sandbox_permissions` (the narrowest wider mode that suffices) plus a one-sentence `justification`. Do not detour through chat to ask permission first — the approval prompt raised by that retry is how the user consents. If the session states approval prompts are disabled, there is no exception: a denial is final — do not set `sandbox_permissions`. Never escalate speculatively: ground the request in a real denial — normally the one this command just hit; escalating up front is fine only when this session already denied the same access. A rejected escalation is final for that command — stop and explain, never work around it — but it does not forbid attempting or escalating other commands later.

description.description: Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice, 5-10 words (shown in the UI). Examples: "ls" → "List files in current directory"; "git status" → "Show working tree status"; "npm install" → "Install package dependencies".

timeoutMs.description: Timeout in milliseconds. The executor applies its configured default and cap, and kills the command on expiry.

workdir.description: Working directory for this command. Defaults to the session workspace; a relative path is resolved against it.

run_in_background.description: Run in the background and return a job id immediately (collect with job_output, stop with job_kill). No timeout applies.

sandbox_permissions.description: The wider sandbox mode this command needs. Only valid as a one-shot retry of a command the sandbox just denied; requires justification and user approval.

justification.description: Required with sandbox_permissions: one sentence for the user explaining why this exact command needs the wider access.

`src/cli.js` is the program; how the work is split across other files under `src/` is up to you. It takes exactly one argument, `expand` or `match`, and reads UTF-8 text from standard input. Split the input on newlines and drop the empty tail a trailing newline leaves. In `expand` mode the input must be exactly one line, the pattern, and the output is its brace expansions, one per line, in order, keeping duplicates. In `match` mode the first line is the pattern and every later line is a candidate path; print one line per candidate, `+ `, then the candidate, when it matches, and `- `, then the candidate, when it does not. A pattern with no candidates prints nothing. Exit 0 on success.

Brace expansion runs before matching, and a pattern matches when any of its expansions does. Find the leftmost `{` that has a matching `}`, counting nesting and skipping any character preceded by a backslash. Split the text between them on the commas that sit at that group's own nesting depth, again skipping escaped characters. If there is at least one such comma, the parts are the alternatives, and an alternative may be empty. If there is none, read the body as a range: `A..B` or `A..B..S` where both endpoints are integers, optionally signed, or both are single ASCII letters. The step is the absolute value of `S`, defaulting to 1, and a step of 0 makes the body not a range. Values run from the first endpoint towards the second, inclusive, walking code points for letters, so `{e..a}` counts down and `{A..d}` passes through the characters that lie between `Z` and `a`. An integer range pads its values with leading zeros to the width of the longer endpoint's digits when either endpoint is written with a leading zero, placing the sign before the padding. A body that is neither a list nor a range leaves its braces as literal text, and the search for the next group resumes just after that `{`. A `{` with no matching `}` is literal too. Each alternative is substituted for the whole group and the result expanded again, so the leftmost group varies slowest.

Matching splits both the pattern and the path on `/`, skipping an escaped `/`, and compares segment by segment; a pattern segment that is exactly `**` instead matches zero or more whole path segments, none of which may begin with `.`. Any other segment must match its path segment as a whole. Within a segment, `\` makes the next character literal, `?` matches exactly one character, and any run of `*` matches zero or more characters. A bracket class opens with `[`, is negated by a leading `!` or `^`, holds single characters and `from-to` code-point ranges, treats a `]` written first as a literal, treats a `-` that has no character after it as a literal, honours a backslash inside itself, and closes at the first `]` that is neither first nor escaped. An extended group is one of `?`, `*`, `+`, `@` or `!` immediately followed by `(`, holding `|`-separated sub-patterns and closing at its matching `)`; sub-patterns may themselves hold groups. `?(…)` matches zero or one of its alternatives, `*(…)` zero or more, `+(…)` one or more, `@(…)` exactly one, and `!(…)` matches any run of characters that is not one of them. All five may be followed by more pattern, and the segment matches when some division of the text satisfies the whole segment.

A path segment that begins with `.` matches only a pattern segment whose first element is a literal `.`, written plainly or escaped; a wildcard, a class or a group at the start of a segment never matches that dot. Neither `?`, nor `*`, nor a class, nor a group ever matches a `/`, because matching is done inside one segment.

A failure writes one line to standard error and exits 2, having written nothing to standard output. The messages are `error: usage: cli.js expand|match` when the arguments are not exactly one of the two mode words; `error: expand needs exactly one pattern line` when `expand` receives any number of lines other than one; `error: match needs a pattern line` when `match` receives no line at all; `error: unterminated bracket in pattern` when a `[` has no closing `]`; `error: unterminated extglob in pattern` when a group has no closing `)`; `error: trailing backslash in pattern` when a backslash ends the pattern or a class; and `error: range is too long` when a range would produce more than 1000 values.
